The United States Senate. One of two chambers of the U.S. Congress, established by the Constitution as the upper house of the legislative branch with two senators per state. Designed as a more deliberative body than the House of Representatives, the Senate holds unique powers including treaty ratification, impeachment trials, and Supreme Court confirmation.

The Constitution established the Senate with two senators per state, regardless of population, giving every state equal representation in the upper chamber and protecting smaller states' interests. Initially, senators were elected by state legislatures, not by popular vote. The seventeenth Amendment in nineteen thirteen shifted power to direct popular election, democratizing Senate selection.

The Senate holds exclusive powers to ratify treaties, which require a two-thirds supermajority, confirm presidential appointments including cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and Supreme Court justices, and try impeachment cases. The filibuster rule allows senators to delay or prevent votes through extended debate. Breaking a filibuster requires a sixty-vote supermajority to invoke cloture, giving obstruction formidable power.

Reconstruction-era amendments and voting rights acts opened the Senate to Black senators like Hiram Revels in eighteen seventy and Blanche Bruce in eighteen seventy-five, though segregation and discrimination delayed true integration for a century. The Senate has undergone periodic constitutional crises when presidents faced impeachment trials, most notably Andrew Johnson in eighteen sixty-eight, Richard Nixon who resigned in nineteen seventy-four, and Donald Trump in twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-four.

The Senate operates with one hundred members total, fifty states with two senators each. Each senator serves a six-year staggered term, with roughly one-third elected every two years, ensuring continuity and resistance to electoral waves.
